clinicalPearls: A chronic destructive granulomatous infection of the kidney in which lipid-laden foamy macrophages progressively replace the parenchyma.
It is strongly associated with chronic obstruction, typically a staghorn calculus, and recurrent infection.
Proteus mirabilis and Escherichia coli are the commonest organisms.
It is usually unilateral and presents with flank pain, fever, malaise, weight loss, a palpable mass and recurrent urinary infections.
The classic bear-paw sign on CT shows an enlarged non-functioning kidney with dilated calyces around a central calculus.
It mimics renal cell carcinoma radiologically and histologically, so the diagnosis is often confirmed only after nephrectomy.
It may form fistulae (nephrocutaneous or reno-colic) and involve the perinephric space and psoas muscle.
Definitive treatment is usually total nephrectomy, with partial nephrectomy occasionally suitable for focal disease.
reference.pathophysiology: Xanthogranulomatous pyelonephritis is a chronic granulomatous inflammatory response to long-standing renal infection in the setting of obstruction, typically a calculus, and impaired urinary drainage. Persistent bacterial infection with incomplete clearance provokes accumulation of lipid-laden foamy macrophages (xanthoma cells) mixed with other inflammatory cells, which progressively destroy and replace the renal parenchyma. The process may extend beyond the capsule into perinephric fat, the psoas muscle and adjacent organs and can generate fistulae, mimicking malignant infiltration both radiologically and macroscopically.
additionalInvestigations: Contrast CT showing the bear-paw sign, staghorn calculus and a non-functioning kidney
Full blood count (anaemia, leucocytosis) and renal function
DMSA or MAG3 renography for differential renal function
Imaging for fistulae and perinephric extension
Histology of the nephrectomy specimen (definitive, showing foam cells)
redFlags: Sepsis from an obstructed infected kidney (pyonephrosis)
Diagnostic uncertainty with possible renal malignancy
reference.prognosis: The prognosis is excellent after complete surgical removal of the affected kidney, with low recurrence; morbidity relates chiefly to the extent of local invasion, fistulae and perioperative complications.
pitfalls: Misdiagnosing the condition as renal cell carcinoma, or vice versa
Underestimating perinephric extension that complicates surgery
Attempting nephron-sparing surgery in diffuse disease
Inadequate perioperative treatment of sepsis and obstruction
management: Nephrectomy, usually total removal of the non-functioning kidney together with any staghorn calculus, is the definitive treatment
Give targeted antibiotics guided by urine and blood cultures, covering Proteus mirabilis and Escherichia coli, to control infection before and after surgery
Relieve obstruction and drain any perinephric collection or abscess, with pre-operative optimisation of sepsis and correction of anaemia and nutritional deficits
Confirm the non-functioning kidney with DMSA or MAG3 renography and safeguard the function of the contralateral kidney
Manage local extension into perinephric fat, psoas or adjacent organs and any fistulae at operation, with wider resection if renal cell carcinoma cannot be excluded
Coordinate urology, interventional radiology and microbiology in a multidisciplinary approach
Escalate emergently in urosepsis with resuscitation, source control and broad-spectrum antimicrobials pending cultures
